claim: SARS-CoV-2 has led to a worldwide pandemic of COVID-19.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a worldwide pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) (Coronaviridae Study Group of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses, 2020; World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to authoritative sources (Coronaviridae Study Group and WHO).

claim: ACE2 is a host receptor of SARS-CoV-2.
source: As a host receptor of SARS-CoV-2, the expression level of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) has been found to influence both the risk and severity of infection (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2003; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The expression level of ACE2 influences both the risk and severity of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: As a host receptor of SARS-CoV-2, the expression level of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) has been found to influence both the risk and severity of infection (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Li et al., 2003; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: There is substantial disparity in the susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Moreover, a growing body of evidence from epidemiological investigations has demonstrated a substantial disparity in the susceptibility to infection (Guan et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020; Mehra et al., 2020; Patanavanich and Glantz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Current smokers have an increased risk of in-hospital death from COVID-19 compared with ever-smokers or non-smokers (OR=1.79; 95% CI: 1.29–2.47).
source: For example, a multi-center study involving 8910 COVID-19 cases from 169 hospitals in Europe and North America identified an increased risk of in-hospital death among current smokers (odds ratio [OR]=1.79; 95% CI: 1.29–2.47) compared with ever-smokers or non-smokers (Mehra et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a multi-center observational study.

claim: Smokers expressed a significantly higher level of ACE2 compared to non-smokers in both European and Asian ancestry populations in lung cancer tissues.
source: Consistent with findings from large-scale population-based observational studies, a laboratory-based study involving 131 RNA-sequenced human lung cancer tissues (54 samples of European ancestry individuals and 77 samples of Asian ancestry individuals) found that smokers expressed a significantly higher level of ACE2 compared to non-smokers in both populations, leading to a potentially heightened susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection (Cai, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a laboratory study with RNA-sequencing data.

claim: The significant smoking-ACE2 association observed in 224 lung cancer samples did not alter after adjusting for age, sex, race, and platforms.
source: Furthermore, incorporating two additional DNA microarray datasets of lung cancer, the significant smoking-ACE2 association observed in a total of 224 samples did not alter after adjusting for age, sex, race, and platforms.
evidence: Supported by reference to analysis incorporating additional datasets with statistical adjustment.

claim: Samples from lung cancer patients restrict generalizability to normal lung tissues and to the general population.
source: Nevertheless, these samples are derived from lung cancer patients, restricting its generalizability to normal lung tissues and to the general population.
evidence: Based on logical inference about study limitations.

claim: Rao et al. identified several exposures including diabetes, breast cancer, lung cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and smoking to increase ACE2 expression in normal lung tissue.
source: In a related work, Rao et al. conducted a phenome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) study examining an extensive amount of diseases, traits, and blood proteins and identified several 'exposures' including diabetes, breast cancer, lung cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and smoking to increase ACE2 expression in normal lung tissue (Rao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published MR study.

claim: Rao et al. used only three SNPs as instrumental variables for smoking, which explained negligible phenotypic variation and did not accurately predict smoking status.
source: However, regarding smoking, only three single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were used as instrumental variables (IVs) by Rao et al., which explained negligible phenotypic variation and did not accurately predict smoking status.
evidence: Based on inference about the limitations of the cited study's methodology.

claim: The hitherto largest GWAS of tobacco use was conducted in a total of 1.2 million individuals and discovered over 400 genetic variants associated with smoking initiation and intensity.
source: The hitherto largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) of tobacco use was conducted in a total of 1.2 million individuals and discovered over 400 genetic variants associated with smoking initiation and intensity (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a large-scale GWAS.

claim: Rao et al. focused on lung tissue instead of systemically examining all human tissues.
source: Last but not least, Rao et al. focused on lung tissue instead of systemically examining all human tissues.
evidence: Based on inference about the scope of the cited study.

claim: Recent studies have identified the involvement of other human tissues (e.g. gastrointestinal tract) in SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Despite lungs being the most relevant and vulnerable organ to a respiratory syndrome COVID-19, recent studies have identified the involvement of other human tissues (e.g. gastrointestinal tract) in SARS-CoV-2 infection (Zou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: GTEx collects a large variety of tissues (N=44) from healthy population (deceased donors).
source: As one of the hitherto largest databases with concomitant information on DNA genotype and RNA expression, GTEx collects a large variety of tissues (N=44) from healthy population (deceased donors) (Gamazon et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to the GTEx database description.

claim: Data on COVID-19 susceptibility and severity were obtained from COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative.
source: In addition, data on COVID-19 susceptibility and severity were obtained from COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, a global project aims to understand the role of host genome in COVID-19 outcome (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to the data source.

claim: IV-exposure associations were extracted from the hitherto largest GWAS conducted by the GCSCAN consortium for tobacco use and alcohol consumption, totalling 1.2 million individuals of European ancestry.
source: IV-exposure associations were extracted from the hitherto largest GWAS conducted by the GCSCAN consortium (GWAS and Sequencing Consortium of Alcohol and Nicotine use) for tobacco use and alcohol consumption, totalling 1.2 million individuals of European ancestry (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to the GWAS data source.

claim: 378 independent SNPs were used as instrumental variables for smoking initiation (N=1,232,091).
source: In our analysis, we included two smoking phenotypes and one drinking phenotype, smoking initiation as reflected by never vs. ever smoking (IV=378, N=1,232,091), smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day (IV=55, N=337,334), and common (opposing to excessive or harmful) alcohol drinking behaviour defined as drinks per week (IV=99, N=941,280).
evidence: Directly stated data about the study design.

claim: 55 independent SNPs were used as instrumental variables for cigarettes per day (N=337,334).
source: In our analysis, we included two smoking phenotypes and one drinking phenotype, smoking initiation as reflected by never vs. ever smoking (IV=378, N=1,232,091), smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day (IV=55, N=337,334), and common (opposing to excessive or harmful) alcohol drinking behaviour defined as drinks per week (IV=99, N=941,280).
evidence: Directly stated data about the study design.

claim: 99 independent SNPs were used as instrumental variables for drinks per week (N=941,280).
source: In our analysis, we included two smoking phenotypes and one drinking phenotype, smoking initiation as reflected by never vs. ever smoking (IV=378, N=1,232,091), smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day (IV=55, N=337,334), and common (opposing to excessive or harmful) alcohol drinking behaviour defined as drinks per week (IV=99, N=941,280).
evidence: Directly stated data about the study design.

claim: The proportion of phenotypic variance explained by IVs accounted for 2.3% for smoking initiation, 1.1% for cigarettes per day, and 0.2% for drinks per week.
source: The proportion of phenotypic variance explained by IVs accounted for 2.3% for smoking initiation, 1.1% for cigarettes per day, and 0.2% for drinks per week.
evidence: Directly stated statistical data from the analysis.

claim: The F-statistics for smoking initiation, smoking intensity (cigarettes per day), and alcohol consumption (drinks per week) were 77.2, 67.4, and 17.8, respectively, indicating strong IVs (F-statistics > 10).
source: The F-statistics for smoking initiation, smoking intensity (cigarettes per day), and alcohol consumption (drinks per week) were 77.2, 67.4, and 17.8, respectively, indicating strong IVs (F-statistics > 10) for each of our exposure of interest.
evidence: Directly stated statistical data with interpretation based on established criteria.

claim: The study focused on ACE2 expression in 44 tissues/organs with at least 100 individuals to ensure statistical power.
source: Out of the total 54 tissues/organs, we focused on ACE2 expression in 44 tissues/organs with a decent sample size involving at least 100 individuals to ensure statistical power (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Directly stated methodological decision based on statistical considerations.

claim: ACE2 RNA and protein quantities have been found to be well correlated in tissues such as lung and kidney.
source: Since ACE2 RNA and protein quantities have been found to be well correlated in tissues such as lung and kidney (Wang et al., 2020), ACE2 RNA expression acts as a good proxy for ACE2 protein expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: ACE2 RNA expression acts as a good proxy for ACE2 protein expression.
source: Since ACE2 RNA and protein quantities have been found to be well correlated in tissues such as lung and kidney (Wang et al., 2020), ACE2 RNA expression acts as a good proxy for ACE2 protein expression.
evidence: Based on inference from cited correlation data.

claim: COVID-19 susceptibility cases were defined as individuals with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection, clinician diagnosis, health record evidence by ICD coding, or self-reported (Ncase=38,984 vs. Ncontrol=1,644,784).
source: Briefly, susceptibility to COVID-19 cases was defined as individuals with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection (via nucleic acid amplification test or serological test), clinician diagnosis, health record evidence by ICD coding, or self-reported (Ncase=38,984 vs. Ncontrol=1,644,784).
evidence: Directly stated definition and sample sizes from the study.

claim: Hospitalized COVID-19 cases were defined as individuals hospitalized due to COVID-19 related symptoms with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection (Ncase=9986 vs. Ncontrol=1,877,672).
source: Hospitalized COVID-19 cases were defined as individuals hospitalized due to COVID-19 related symptoms with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection (Ncase=9986 vs. Ncontrol=1,877,672).
evidence: Directly stated definition and sample sizes from the study.

claim: Very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 cases were defined as hospitalized individuals with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection, who needed respiratory support except for simple oxygen supplementary or died due to COVID-19 (Ncase=5101 vs. Ncontrol=1,383,241).
source: Very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 cases were defined as hospitalized individuals with laboratory-confirmed positive for SARS-Cov-2 infection, who needed respiratory support except for simple oxygen supplementary or died due to COVID-19 (Ncase=5101 vs. Ncontrol=1,383,241).
evidence: Directly stated definition and sample sizes from the study.

claim: MR uses SNPs as proxies for exposure(s) assuming that SNPs are randomly allotted at conception mirroring a randomized procedure and that SNPs always precede disease onset to eliminate reverse causality.
source: MR uses SNPs as proxies for exposure(s) assuming that SNPs are randomly allotted at conception mirroring a randomized procedure and that SNPs always precede disease onset to eliminate reverse causality.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MR methodology.

claim: Three essential model assumptions need to be fulfilled to guarantee valid IVs: IVs are associated with the exposure (relevance assumption); there is no association between IVs and any confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship (independence assumption); and IVs are associated with the outcome only through the studied exposure (exclusion restriction assumption).
source: Three essential model assumptions need to be fulfilled to guarantee valid IVs (Zheng et al., 2017), that is, IVs are associated with the exposure (relevance assumption); there is no association between IVs and any confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship (independence assumption); and IVs are associated with the outcome only through the studied exposure (exclusion restriction assumption).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MR methodology, supported by citation.

claim: Genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in brain putamen basal ganglia (β=1.117, p=0.006).
source: We found that genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in brain putamen basal ganglia (β=1.117, p=0.006), in brain hypothalamus (β=0.848, p=0.022), and in subcutaneous adipose tissue (β=0.285, p=0.016) using the IVW approach (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in brain hypothalamus (β=0.848, p=0.022).
source: We found that genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in brain putamen basal ganglia (β=1.117, p=0.006), in brain hypothalamus (β=0.848, p=0.022), and in subcutaneous adipose tissue (β=0.285, p=0.016) using the IVW approach (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in subcutaneous adipose tissue (β=0.285, p=0.016).
source: We found that genetically instrumented smoking initiation was associated with a significantly increased ACE2 expression in brain putamen basal ganglia (β=1.117, p=0.006), in brain hypothalamus (β=0.848, p=0.022), and in subcutaneous adipose tissue (β=0.285, p=0.016) using the IVW approach (Table 1).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Increased ACE2 expression in transverse colon (β=1.129, p=0.017) was observed through the MR-Egger regression for smoking initiation.
source: Additionally, increased ACE2 expression in two colon tissues was observed only through the MR-Egger regression (transverse colon [β=1.129, p=0.017] and sigmoid colon [β=1.925, p=0.042]) and the direction of estimates remained consistent in the IVW approach.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR-Egger regression analysis.

claim: Increased ACE2 expression in sigmoid colon (β=1.925, p=0.042) was observed through the MR-Egger regression for smoking initiation.
source: Additionally, increased ACE2 expression in two colon tissues was observed only through the MR-Egger regression (transverse colon [β=1.129, p=0.017] and sigmoid colon [β=1.925, p=0.042]) and the direction of estimates remained consistent in the IVW approach.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR-Egger regression analysis.

claim: Horizontal pleiotropy was observed in transverse colon by MR-Egger intercept (p=0.04) for smoking initiation.
source: For all these associations, we did not find apparent heterogeneity as indicated by Cochran's Q statistics (all p>0.05) or horizontal pleiotropy as indicted by MR-Egger intercept (all p>0.05) and MR-PRESSO global test (all p>1.0×10−6), except that horizontal pleiotropy was observed in transverse colon by MR-Egger intercept (p=0.04).
evidence: Directly stated results from the pleiotropy test.

claim: Genetically predicted smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in thyroid (β=1.468, p=1.8×10−8).
source: We further identified that genetically predicted smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in thyroid (β=1.468, p=1.8×10−8), in liver (β=1.216, p=0.009), in brain hypothalamus (β=1.789, p=0.014), and in ovary (β=1.545, p=0.026) using the IVW method (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Genetically predicted smoking intensity was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in liver (β=1.216, p=0.009).
source: We further identified that genetically predicted smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in thyroid (β=1.468, p=1.8×10−8), in liver (β=1.216, p=0.009), in brain hypothalamus (β=1.789, p=0.014), and in ovary (β=1.545, p=0.026) using the IVW method (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Genetically predicted smoking intensity was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in brain hypothalamus (β=1.789, p=0.014).
source: We further identified that genetically predicted smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in thyroid (β=1.468, p=1.8×10−8), in liver (β=1.216, p=0.009), in brain hypothalamus (β=1.789, p=0.014), and in ovary (β=1.545, p=0.026) using the IVW method (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Genetically predicted smoking intensity was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in ovary (β=1.545, p=0.026).
source: We further identified that genetically predicted smoking intensity as reflected by cigarettes per day was associated with a significantly elevated ACE2 expression in thyroid (β=1.468, p=1.8×10−8), in liver (β=1.216, p=0.009), in brain hypothalamus (β=1.789, p=0.014), and in ovary (β=1.545, p=0.026) using the IVW method (Table 2).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claim: Levels of ACE2 expression decreased with genetically instrumented smoking intensity in sigmoid colon tissue (β=−1.971, p=0.019) using the MR-Egger regression.
source: On the contrary, levels of ACE2 expression decreased with genetically instrumented smoking intensity in sigmoid colon tissue (β=−1.971, p=0.019) and in vagina tissue (β=−3.271, p=0.043) using the MR-Egger regression.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR-Egger regression analysis.

claim: Levels of ACE2 expression decreased with genetically instrumented smoking intensity in vagina tissue (β=−3.271, p=0.043) using the MR-Egger regression.
source: On the contrary, levels of ACE2 expression decreased with genetically instrumented smoking intensity in sigmoid colon tissue (β=−1.971, p=0.019) and in vagina tissue (β=−3.271, p=0.043) using the MR-Egger regression.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR-Egger regression analysis.

claim: Only one suggestive association with ACE2 expression in tibial nerve was observed for alcohol consumption using the IVW approach (β=−1.462, p=0.006).
source: For alcohol consumption defined as drinks per week, only one suggestive association with ACE2 expression in tibial nerve was observed using the IVW approach (β=−1.462, p=0.006).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis.

claim: Smoking initiation significantly increased the risk of COVID-19 onset (IVW: OR=1.15, 95%CI: 1.07–1.23, p=8.7×10−5).
source: We found that smoking initiation significantly increased the risk of COVID-19 onset (IVW: OR=1.15, 95%CI: 1.07–1.23, p=8.7×10−5) even after taking into account multiple comparisons (Table 3).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis, with reference to Table 3.

claim: Smoking initiation increased the risk of very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 using the IVW approach.
source: In addition, smoking initiation increased the risk of very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 and hospitalized COVID-19 using the IVW approach, but the results were not supported by the MR-Egger regression.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis with noted limitation.

claim: Smoking initiation increased the risk of hospitalized COVID-19 using the IVW approach.
source: In addition, smoking initiation increased the risk of very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 and hospitalized COVID-19 using the IVW approach, but the results were not supported by the MR-Egger regression.
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR analysis with noted limitation.

claim: Smoking intensity (cigarettes per day) increased the risk of very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 as shown in the MR-Egger regression (OR=5.99, 95%CI: 1.57–22.84, p=0.012).
source: Smoking intensity (cigarettes per day) only increased the risk of very severe respiratory confirmed COVID-19 as shown in the MR-Egger regression (OR=5.99, 95%CI: 1.57–22.84, p=0.012) (Supplementary file 1o).
evidence: Directly stated results from the MR-Egger regression analysis.

claim: No causal link was found between alcohol consumption (drinks per week) and the risk of COVID-19 adverse outcomes.
source: On the contrary, we did not find a causal link between alcohol consumption (drinks per week) and the risk of COVID-19 adverse outcomes (Supplementary file 1p).
evidence: Directly stated null finding from the MR analysis.

claim: A study involving 214 patients with laboratory confirmed COVID-19 from Wenzhou China found that patients with severe disease were more likely to be smokers (26.3% vs. 6.4%, p = 0.038) compared to non-severe cases.
source: For example, a study involving 214 patients with laboratory confirmed COVID-19 from Wenzhou China found that compared to non-severe cases, patients with severe disease were more likely to be smokers (26.3% vs. 6.4%, p = 0.038) (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to an observational study.

claim: A study recruiting 78 patients with COVID-19 in Wuhan found a higher proportion of ever-smokers in COVID-19 progression group than in the improvement/stabilization group (OR=14.28, 95% CI:1.58–25.00, p=0.018).
source: Another study recruiting 78 patients with COVID-19 in Wuhan also found a higher proportion of ever-smokers in COVID-19 progression group than in the improvement/stabilization group (OR=14.28, 95% CI:1.58–25.00, p=0.018) (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to an observational study.

claim: A meta-analysis on 11,590 COVID-19 cases demonstrated a higher proportion of smokers among 2133 patients who experienced disease progression, suggesting that smoking aggravated COVID-19 progression (OR=1.91, 95% CI: 1.42–2.59).
source: Consistent with these findings, a meta-analysis on a total of 11,590 COVID-19 cases demonstrated a higher proportion of smokers among 2133 patients experienced disease progression, suggesting that smoking aggravated COVID-19 progression (OR=1.91, 95% CI: 1.42–2.59) (Patanavanich and Glantz, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: A retrospective study including 191 patients found a comparable proportion of smokers in survivors and non-survivors (9% vs. 4%, p=0.21).
source: For instance, a retrospective study including 191 patients of which 137 survived and 54 non-survived found a comparable proportion of smokers in survivors and non-survivors (9% vs. 4%, p=0.21) (Zhou et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to an observational study.

claim: A meta-analysis including five studies involving 1399 individuals with COVID-19 revealed no significant association between smoking and disease severity (OR=1.69, 95% CI: 0.41–6.92).
source: A meta-analysis including five studies (four in Wuhan and one across 30 provinces in Mainland China) (Guan et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) involving 1399 individuals with COVID-19 revealed no significant association between smoking and disease severity (OR=1.69, 95% CI: 0.41–6.92) (Lippi and Henry, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: Evidence from the Veterans Affairs Birth Cohort in a US population found that current smoking was associated with a lower risk of COVID-19 susceptibility (OR=0.45, 95% CI: 0.35–0.57).
source: Opposite to the findings from Asian population, evidence from the Veterans Affairs Birth Cohort in a US population found that current smoking was associated with a lower risk of COVID-19 susceptibility (OR=0.45, 95% CI: 0.35–0.57) (Rentsch et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to an observational study.

claim: Only 1.4% patients were current smokers in the study conducted by Zhang et al., 2020.
source: For example, compared with the high proportion of smokers in China (an average 26.6% prevalence in the general population), only 1.4% patients were current smokers in the study conducted by Zhang et al., 2020 and 12.6% in the study conducted by Guan et al., 2020.
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Only 12.6% patients were current smokers in the study conducted by Guan et al., 2020.
source: For example, compared with the high proportion of smokers in China (an average 26.6% prevalence in the general population), only 1.4% patients were current smokers in the study conducted by Zhang et al., 2020 and 12.6% in the study conducted by Guan et al., 2020.
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Cai et al. identified that smoking was associated with an elevated expression of ACE2 in the lung.
source: For example, Cai et al. identified that smoking was associated with an elevated expression of ACE2 in the lung, providing biological evidence of smoking with an increased susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection or severity (Cai, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a laboratory study.

claim: Rao et al. identified a nominal significant association between tobacco use and ACE2 expression in the lung (IVW: β=0.918, p=0.016).
source: Moreover, Rao et al. conducted a phenome-wide MR study incorporating 3948 traits, diseases, and blood proteins and identified a nominal significant association between tobacco use and ACE2 expression in the lung (IVW: β=0.918, p=0.016) (Rao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a published MR study.

claim: The association between tobacco use and ACE2 expression in the lung identified by Rao et al. did not pass multiple comparisons (p-value for FDR was 0.51).
source: However, this association did not pass multiple comparisons (p-value for FDR was 0.51), which was consistent with our MR results using a greatly augmented number of IVs (for smoking status IV=378).
evidence: Directly stated statistical result with comparison to the current study.

claim: ACE2 is a type I transmembrane metallocarboxypeptidase homologous to ACE.
source: As a type I transmembrane metallocarboxypeptidase homologous to ACE, ACE2 is known to be expressed in a variety of tissues, including respiratory tract, cardio-renal tissues, and gastrointestinal tissues (Harmer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research and established knowledge.

claim: ACE2 is known to be expressed in a variety of tissues, including respiratory tract, cardio-renal tissues, and gastrointestinal tissues.
source: As a type I transmembrane metallocarboxypeptidase homologous to ACE, ACE2 is known to be expressed in a variety of tissues, including respiratory tract, cardio-renal tissues, and gastrointestinal tissues (Harmer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: Enrichment of SARS-CoV-2 in gastrointestinal tract has been confirmed by testing viral RNA in stool from 71 patients with COVID-19.
source: While SARS-CoV-2 mainly spreads via respiratory tract, enrichment of SARS-CoV-2 in gastrointestinal tract has been confirmed by testing viral RNA in stool from 71 patients with COVID-19, suggesting the importance of gastrointestinal involvement in the infection (Xiao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study with viral RNA testing data.

claim: Nearly one-fifth COVID-19 patients remained SARS-CoV-2 RNA-positive in their stool, despite negative results in their respiratory samples.
source: Furthermore, nearly one-fifth COVID-19 patients remained SARS-CoV-2 RNA-positive in their stool, despite negative results in their respiratory samples.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited study data.

claim: ACE2 was abundantly expressed in the gastrointestinal epithelia, but rarely expressed in the esophageal epithelia in COVID-19 patients.
source: Of those 71 patients, ACE2 was abundantly expressed in the gastrointestinal epithelia, but rarely expressed in the esophageal epithelia.
evidence: Based on inference from the cited study data.

claim: Findings from public databases (GEO, GTEx, and HPA) have demonstrated a higher expression level of ACE2 in the gastrointestinal tract (colon, rectal, and small intestine) and liver than in the lung.
source: In addition, findings from public databases (GEO, GTEx, and HPA) have demonstrated a higher expression level of ACE2 in the gastrointestinal tract (colon, rectal, and small intestine) and liver than in the lung (Burgueño et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Pirola and Sookoian, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies analyzing public databases.

claim: Smoking may promote cellular uptake of SARS-CoV-2 through nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) signalling.
source: Smoking may promote cellular uptake of SARS-CoV-2 through nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) signalling (Russo et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research, presented as speculation.

claim: nAChR and ACE2 are known to be co-expressed on many sites such as cortex, striatum, and hypothalamus within human brain.
source: It is worth noting that nAChR and ACE2 are known to be co-expressed on many sites such as cortex, striatum, and hypothalamus within human brain (Dani and Bertrand, 2007; Jones et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research.

claim: Nicotine stimulation of the nAChR increased ACE2 expression within neural cells.
source: Nicotine stimulation of the nAChR increased ACE2 expression within neural cells, indicating a likelihood that smokers are more vulnerable to COVID-19 (Olds and Kabbani, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published research.

claim: GWAS-identified SNPs for smoking and alcohol consumption explained only a small fraction (1–2%) of phenotypic variance.
source: Although hundreds of SNPs were used as proxies for cigarette smoking and alcohol consumption, these GWAS-identified SNPs explained only a small fraction (1–2%) of phenotypic variance.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: The minimum sample size of 114 in brain substantia nigra tissue limited the statistical power of MR analysis.
source: In addition, the minimum sample size of 114 in brain substantia nigra tissue further limited the statistical power of MR analysis, albeit GTEx database is so far the largest available database with both genotype and expression data.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: Data on the genotypes, tissue expression, and COVID-19 related outcomes were all based on European ancestry populations, restricting generalizability to other ethnicities.
source: Moreover, data on the genotypes, tissue expression, and COVID-19 related outcomes of our analyses were all based on European ancestry populations, restricting its generalizability to other ethnicities.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: Few of the significant associations passed the stringent Bonferroni corrections.
source: Finally, we have to acknowledge that few of our significant associations passed the stringent Bonferroni corrections.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: Genetically instrumented smoking phenotypes reflected by both smoking initiation and smoking intensity are significantly associated with a high expression level of ACE2 in multiple tissues/organs.
source: In conclusion, genetically instrumented smoking phenotypes reflected by both smoking initiation and smoking intensity are significantly associated with a high expression level of ACE2 in multiple tissues/organs, subsequently increasing the susceptibility and severity of COVID-19.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's MR analysis results.

claim: Genetically instrumented smoking phenotypes increase the susceptibility and severity of COVID-19.
source: In conclusion, genetically instrumented smoking phenotypes reflected by both smoking initiation and smoking intensity are significantly associated with a high expression level of ACE2 in multiple tissues/organs, subsequently increasing the susceptibility and severity of COVID-19.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's MR analysis results.

claim: Smokers might be more vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection or severe disease.
source: Our results provide important clinical implications on that smokers might be more vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection or severe disease.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings.

claim: Smoking cessation is an important actionable prevention strategy to COVID-19 at the population level.
source: At the population level, smoking cessation is also an important actionable prevention strategy to COVID-19.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's findings about smoking and COVID-19.

claim: 80-95% of instrumental variables were successfully mapped to the GTEx database and to the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative database.
source: We were able to map 80–95% of those IVs to the GTEx database and to the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative database – a virtually complete coverage.
evidence: Directly stated data about the study's methodology.

claim: The study had sufficient power (>80%) to detect a causal effect of 0.74–2.66 in ACE2 expression.
source: Under the current sample size, given 1–2% of the phenotypic variance of smoking and alcohol consumption explained by IVs, our study had sufficient power (>80%) to detect a causal effect of 0.74–2.66 in ACE2 expression, and to detect an OR ranging from 1.11 to 1.39 for COVID-19 related outcomes (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Directly stated power calculation results.
